title: Pest Control CRM: Six Tools That Track Leads and Renewals
html:
A pest control CRM should track every lead, every recurring service plan and every renewal in one place. Most pest companies run a field service app such as Jobber or GorillaDesk and add a free sales CRM such as HubSpot. Pair the system with steady lead generation so it has new customers to work. Published plans in this guide run from free to $149 a month, and two vendors publish no price at all.

A pest control CRM has to do three jobs: catch the lead, schedule the recurring visit and flag the renewal. Pest work is repeat work. One customer who signs a recurring plan is worth more than a single treatment, so the system must remember them long after the first visit. This guide sorts six tools by the job each one does, with the price each vendor publishes and one real limit for each.

A missed callback is the most common reason to buy a CRM, and the cheapest one to prevent. If a lead never gets a reply, no software setting will save it.

Which pest control CRM handles routes and recurring service?

GorillaDesk and FieldRoutes are the two names in this guide built around route-based pest work. Both tie customer records to a schedule, which is what a recurring plan needs.

  • GorillaDesk: a field service platform that lists pest control among its industries. Basic is $49 a month, Pro is $99 a month and Growth is $149 a month, each with one route included. Pro adds a customer portal, online booking and QuickBooks Online sync, and Growth adds a sales pipeline and multi-branch support. Limit: it is priced per route, so each extra route adds $30 to $100 a month depending on the plan.
  • FieldRoutes: a pest control platform with lead management, route optimization and a customer payment portal in both of its plans, Growth and Corporate. Limit: the page shows Request Pricing instead of a number, and says the monthly fee is based on active customers. Ask for a written quote before you compare it with anything else.

GorillaDesk states that admin, manager, sales and crew users are free, and only users assigned to a schedule need a paid seat. That matters for a company with a large office team and a few trucks. A route-based price rewards a small, busy crew and punishes a company that adds trucks quickly.

Workiz locks service plans out of Standard, and a recurring pest plan is exactly that. Confirm in a demo that the plan you buy can store a repeat visit with its own interval. Otherwise you will rebuild every renewal by hand.

Jobber's client hub lets customers approve quotes online. For a pest company, that suits a one-time job such as a wasp nest or a rodent exclusion. Check how it handles a plan that repeats, because the vendor does not say.

Which free pest control CRM suits a sales team?

HubSpot CRM is the free pick for a pest company that needs lead tracking before it needs routes. It does not schedule trucks, so it sits beside a field service app and does not replace one.

  • HubSpot CRM: a general sales CRM that lists up to 1,000 contacts and one-to-one email on its Free plan. The Free plan is $0 for up to 2 users with no credit card. Starter starts at $7 per seat a month on annual billing, and the page's FAQ states $10 per seat month to month. Limit: the free plan caps at 2 users, and the page shows two Starter figures, so confirm the one you will pay.

A free CRM earns its place when a company sells pest plans by phone. Log each call, tag the pest type and set a follow-up date. Then a quote sent on Monday gets a reminder on Wednesday without anyone remembering it.

Commercial accounts need their own handling. A restaurant or an apartment complex has several contacts, a contract and a site list. Give those accounts a separate pipeline stage and a named owner. Keep their service notes apart from home plans so a technician sees the right access instructions.

Keep one rule: the field service app owns the customer after the sale, and the sales CRM owns the lead before it. Two systems that both claim the same customer create duplicate records within a month.

Which free tool brings pest control leads into the CRM?

Google Business Profile is the free listing that shows a pest company in Google Maps and local search. Google states that you can add or claim your business at no charge.

  • Google Business Profile: shows your name, service area, photos, reviews and phone number when someone searches for pest control nearby. Limit: it only works when the listing is kept current, and it does not track a lead after the call. See Google's Business Profile help page.

How do you choose a pest control CRM?

Choose a pest control CRM with a three-check filter: fit, cost and setup effort. Run every tool through all three before you pay.

Fit: can it store a recurring plan with its own interval and renewal date? Can it send a reminder before the plan lapses?

Cost: add the plan price, extra routes or users, text credits and card processing. Then compare the total against what one recurring customer pays you in a year.

Setup effort: can one person import the customer list and build service templates in a weekend, or does the vendor need to do it?

A one-truck shop can run HubSpot CRM for lead follow-up, GorillaDesk Basic for scheduling and a free Google Business Profile. That stack lists at $49 a month before add-ons. A multi-branch company that books many routes fits GorillaDesk Growth or FieldRoutes, with a sales CRM kept for commercial accounts.

Two examples show how the stack grows. A pest company with one truck adds a second route in GorillaDesk. The bill then rises by the extra route fee its plan lists. A company that opens a second branch moves to Growth for multi-branch support, or asks FieldRoutes for a quote. Neither move needs a new CRM, because the customer list carries over.

Move up a tier only when a specific task is failing. If callbacks are slipping, add a pipeline. If routes are running long, pay for route optimization. If renewals are lapsing, set reminders first, then upgrade if the system cannot send them.

What should a pest control CRM track from day one?

A pest control CRM should track the lead source, the pest type, the service address, the plan interval and the next visit date. Everything else is secondary.

  • Lead source: record whether the call came from the map listing, a search ad, a referral or a door hanger. Without it you cannot tell which channel pays.
  • Pest type and property type: a termite inspection and a monthly ant plan follow different quote paths. Tag both so reports can split them.
  • Plan interval and renewal date: store the visit rhythm and the date the plan renews. A renewal that nobody sees is a lost customer.
  • Technician notes and photos: the next visit starts from what the last tech found. Notes also help in a complaint.
  • Review request status: mark when you asked for a review and whether it came back.

How should a pest control company follow up leads in the CRM?

Follow up a new pest lead the same business day, and write the rule down so every person on the team applies it. Speed matters because a homeowner with a pest problem often calls more than one company.

  • Call first, then text: a missed call gets a text with your name and a booking link within minutes.
  • Quote with a recurring option: offer the one-time treatment and the recurring plan side by side, so the customer sees the cheaper long-term choice.
  • Set a second touch: every open quote gets a reminder date in the CRM, so a quiet lead gets one more call before it closes.
  • Close the loop: once a plan is signed, move the customer from the sales CRM to the field service app and mark the lead won.

A CRM only follows up when someone sets the reminder. Keep the rules short enough that a new hire can follow them on day one.

Every lead source needs the same intake rules, whether it is paid or organic. Search ads from Google Ads for pest control and rankings from pest control SEO send homeowners to the site. Meta Ads for pest control can reach homeowners before they search.

Reviews feed the same system. Ask right after a completed visit, while the technician's work is fresh, and build that step into the CRM.

What is the best CRM for a pest control company?

There is no single best pick, because it depends on whether you need routes or only sales tracking. GorillaDesk and FieldRoutes are built around pest routes, Jobber suits a small crew, and HubSpot CRM is free for up to 2 users. Test each one against your own recurring plans.

How much does a pest control CRM cost?

Published plans in this guide run from free for HubSpot CRM to $149 a month for GorillaDesk Growth. GorillaDesk Basic and Jobber Core both list at $49 a month. FieldRoutes and Workiz show no price on their pages, so request a written quote before you compare.

Can a pest control CRM track recurring service plans?

Some can and some cannot at every price tier. Workiz locks service plans out of its Standard plan, for example. Ask each vendor to show you a live plan with its own visit interval and renewal date before you sign any contract.

Is HubSpot CRM free for pest control companies?

Yes, for a small team. HubSpot lists a Free plan at $0 for up to 2 users with no credit card required. It lists up to 1,000 contacts and one-to-one email. It does not schedule routes or take payments, so it works beside a field service app.

What should a pest control CRM track first?

Track the lead source, pest type, service address, plan interval and next visit date first. Add the renewal date and technician notes next. Together these fields show which channel pays you and which plans are about to lapse. You can add more fields later, but a long form slows every call.

How fast should a pest control company reply to a new lead?

Reply the same business day at the latest, and make the first call within the hour during business hours when you can. A homeowner with a pest problem often contacts several companies, so a quick reply often wins the plan.
